title: “Householder, suppose near a village or town there is a forest grove. In it there is a tree full of ripe fruits, but none have…
content: “Householder, suppose near a village or town there is a forest grove. In it there is a tree full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen to the ground. Then a man comes, wishing for fruit, seeking fruit, wandering here and there for fruit. He enters that forest, sees that tree full of ripe fruits, and thinks: ‘This tree is full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen. I know how to climb trees. Suppose I climb this tree, eat my fill, and fill my clothes.’ Then he climbs the tree, eats his fill, and fills his clothes. Then a second man comes, wishing for fruit, seeking fruit, wandering here and there for fruit, carrying a sharp axe. He enters that forest, sees that tree full of ripe fruits, and thinks: ‘This tree is full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen. I don’t know how to climb trees. Suppose I cut this tree down at the root, eat my fill, and fill my clothes.’ Then he cuts the tree down at the root. What do you think, householder? If the first man does not climb down quickly, when the tree falls, will it not break his hand, foot, or some part of his body, and will he not thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a fruit tree — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

title: “Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The…
content: “Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The mind arises first for those things, and the unwholesome states follow after.”

title: “Monks, short indeed is the lifespan of humans in this world — one must go on to the future. Do good, live the holy life.…
content:
“Monks, short indeed is the lifespan of humans in this world — one must go on to the future. Do good, live the holy life. For nothing that is born is without death. Monks, a long-lived person lives only a hundred years, or a little more or less.

Human life is short,
The good person should be concerned,
Live as if the head is on fire —
Death will surely come.

Days and nights pass by,
Life span comes to an end,
Human life dries up
Like a stream in the mountains.”

title: “He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that…
content: “He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had delusion — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome.’ Thus, in this very life, he is freed from longing, calm, cooled, experiencing ease, abiding in the Brahma-state himself.”

title: “Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all unarisen evil, unwholesome states are not yet abandoned within him, then he should arouse…
content: “Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all unarisen evil, unwholesome states are not yet abandoned within him, then he should arouse energy to abandon those evil, unwholesome states. Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned within him, then he should dwell with joyful mind, training in wholesome states day and night.”

title: Elder Puṇṇamāsa: Having abandoned the five hindrances, Attaining security from bondage, Holding the mirror of the Dhamma, Knowing and seeing the self. I contemplate this…
content:
Elder Puṇṇamāsa:

Having abandoned the five hindrances,
Attaining security from bondage,
Holding the mirror of the Dhamma,
Knowing and seeing the self.

I contemplate this body,
From within and without —
The body is seen as empty,
Both inside and out.

title: “And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of…
content: “And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. This, monks, is called right effort.”

title: “Monks, have you seen a painting called ‘The Wandering One’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Monks, that painting was created by the mind. Yet the mind is…
content: “Monks, have you seen a painting called ‘The Wandering One’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Monks, that painting was created by the mind. Yet the mind is even more diverse than that painting. Therefore, monks, one should constantly reflect on one’s own mind thus: ‘For a long time, this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion. Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled. Through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.’”

title: “One who has cut off craving, Without remainder, Dried up the swift stream — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like a serpent…
content:
“One who has cut off craving,
Without remainder,
Dried up the swift stream —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One who has destroyed conceit,
Without remainder,
As a great flood destroys a fragile reed —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

title: Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha: Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire. My son, do not share In repeated suffering. Blissful is the…
content:
Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha:

Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire.
My son, do not share
In repeated suffering.

Blissful is the sage,
Without desire, with doubt cut off,
Cooled, self-controlled,
Without any defilements.

That sage practices
The path leading to right view,
Putting an end to suffering.
Vaḍḍha, strive on!

With confidence, mother spoke
This purpose for you —
“My dear mother! I think
That you have no sensual desire.”

“Vaḍḍha, whatever conduct —
Low, high, or middling —
Not even a little sensual desire
Exists in me.

I have destroyed all defilements,
Not heedless, meditating.
The three true knowledges are attained —
The Buddha’s instruction is done.”

Wonderful, my mother,
Encouraging and urging me,
With verses of truth,
Out of compassion.

Hearing my mother’s words,
Her motherly instruction,
I practiced the Dhamma gratefully,
Attaining security from bondage.

I am energetic, striving,
Day and night not lazy.
Well encouraged by my mother,
I attained the supreme purity.
